transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, honestly, I didn't even really want to come in today, but my sister kind of pushed me into it. She thinks I'm stressing myself out too much, but she just doesn't understand what's actually going on. I’m here because... well, for the past year, I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system—like, the actual network where the electronic medical records are kept—is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. 

I'm a phlebotomist, so I know how these things work. I draw blood all day, I see the labels, I know the turnaround times, I know what a complete metabolic panel looks like when it comes back from the lab. And I saw his original results. I saw them with my own eyes before they were officially posted to his patient portal. But then, when I went back to look later, the numbers were different. The creatinine was off, the liver enzymes were just slightly tweaked—not enough for a layman to notice, but enough for someone who knows what they're looking at to see that they've been altered. 

And no matter how many doctors I talk to, or how many times my family members tell me the numbers are fine and that I'm overreacting, I know the chart doesn’t match what I saw. I have copies, I have notes, I've tracked the timestamps of when the files were accessed and modified. It’s wearing me down, it really is. I spend hours every night going over the printouts, cross-referencing the reference ranges, trying to figure out who has the authorization to go into the system and manually overwrite a verified lab result. Because it's not a glitch. A glitch doesn't selectively alter renal function indicators while leaving the lipid panel alone. Someone is doing this intentionally, and nobody will listen to me about it. They just look at me like I'm crazy, but I know what I saw.
Have you ever experienced a time when your mood was unusually high, irritable, or you had so much energy that you didn’t need much sleep?

High? No, definitely not. I mean, my sister tries to tell people I'm acting erratic, but I'm not irritable for no reason, and I'm definitely not walking around with some kind of endless energy. If I'm irritable, it's just because it is incredibly frustrating when you have physical proof of something and people just brush you off. 

And as for sleep... well, I guess I haven't been sleeping very much lately, but it's not because I don't *need* to sleep. I am completely exhausted. I'm so tired my eyes actually burn when I'm at work doing my draws, and my hands feel heavy. I just *can't* sleep because my mind is constantly going over the timestamps on those files. I'll lie down, and then I'll remember that someone accessed the portal at 2:14 AM on a Tuesday, and I have to get up and check my notes to see who was even on shift in the informatics department at that exact hour. 

So, no, I don't have that thing where you feel like you don't need sleep. I desperately need a solid eight hours, I really do. I just can't get it right now because I spend all night staring at these printouts, trying to figure out why they would alter the creatinine levels specifically. Because going from a 1.2 to a 1.5 might not sound like a lot to a receptionist or someone who doesn't look at bloodwork all day, but for renal function, that is a massive discrepancy. Anyone would be losing sleep if they knew someone was tampering with their family member's medical data, right? It’s just normal stress. I'm not high-energy at all, I'm just trying to get to the bottom of this.
Have you ever had the sense that something is being hidden from you, or that a group of people are working together to deceive you or cover something up?

A group? No, I mean... I don't think it's a whole group of people. That sounds like something out of a spy movie, and I'm not... I'm not making things up here. I'm a very logical person. If a whole group of people were working together to deceive me, there would be a massive paper trail. 

In electronic health records—whether a clinic is using Epic or Cerner or whatever system—every single time a file is opened, it leaves a digital footprint. An audit trail. If five or six people were all coordinating to hide my dad's lab results, the access logs would be lighting up like a Christmas tree with different user IDs and terminal locations. But that’s not what I’m seeing. 

I don't think everyone is out to get me. I don't walk down the street thinking people are hiding things from me, and I don't think the doctors themselves are in on it. It's literally just this one, specific issue with the comprehensive metabolic panel. It’s probably just one person. Maybe a careless lab tech who messed up the calibration on the analyzer and didn't want to get written up, or someone in informatics who accidentally merged another patient's data into my dad's file and is trying to cover their tracks so they don't get fired. People do stupid things to save their jobs all the time. 

But it's definitely not a coordinated group effort. My sister keeps saying I'm acting paranoid, like I think the whole hospital is against us, but I keep telling her, 'Look at the timestamps!' If it were a group, the modifications wouldn't just be happening at 2:14 AM on a Tuesday when the network traffic is at its absolute lowest. It would be systematic. But this is targeted. It's just one person hiding their mistake, and I just... I just need to find out who had the login credentials for that specific terminal at that specific time to alter that creatinine value. So, no, I don't feel like there's some big group deception or that people are hiding other things from me. I just want the correct numbers on the chart, and I'm going to keep looking at the printouts until I figure out exactly whose user ID is attached to that overwrite.
Have you ever felt like you’ve lost interest or pleasure in things you used to care about, even things you were really into before?

Well, no, not exactly. I mean, my sister says I've stopped doing things, but it’s not that I’ve lost interest or that I don't care anymore. It’s just... it's a matter of priority, you know? Like, I used to go to this pottery class every Thursday night. I loved it. I was working on this really intricate coil vase, and I had all these plans for the glaze, and I used to really look forward to it. And I used to go hiking on the weekends, too. I had a whole group of friends I’d go with, and we’d do these eight-mile loops up near the state park. 

But how am I supposed to sit there and mold clay, or spend six hours walking in the woods, when I know that someone is actively tampering with a medical record? I can’t. I physically can’t just turn my brain off and pretend everything is fine. Every time I tried to go to pottery after I found the first discrepancy in the lab results, I’d just sit there staring at the wheel, thinking about the reference ranges for liver enzymes. I’d be thinking, 'If the ALT was elevated on the original draw, why did the uploaded chart show it right in the middle of normal limits?' 

So it’s not that I don’t find pleasure in pottery or hiking anymore. If this was all resolved, if I could just get someone to pull the audit logs and show me the user ID that made the change, I’d go back to class tomorrow. I really would. I miss it. But right now, my time is just completely consumed by this. I have to spend my evenings cross-referencing the printouts. I have a whole system set up on my dining room table—color-coded highlighters for different dates, sticky notes for the timestamp anomalies. It takes hours. By the time I’m done, it’s past midnight, and I still have to be at the clinic by 6:30 AM to start my draws. 

So, yeah, I guess I haven’t been doing the things I used to do, but it’s not some kind of depression where I just don't care about life. I care a lot. I care too much, probably. I’m just busy. I have to figure this out, and until I do, everything else just has to take a back seat. I mean, wouldn't you do the same thing if it was your dad's chart? You wouldn't just go hiking and ignore it.
Have you ever been absolutely certain of something that others say isn’t true, even when there was no clear evidence to support it?

Well, see, that’s the thing. You say no clear evidence, but there is evidence, it’s just that no one wants to look at it properly. I mean, this is exactly why I’m even here talking to you in the first place. For the past year—literally an entire twelve months, it started last fall—I have been trying to prove that someone inside the clinic system is either changing or actively holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. 

And everyone, I mean literally everyone, keeps telling me it isn't true. My sister, like I said, she thinks I’m making it all up or seeing things that aren't there. My dad’s primary care doctor actually sighed at me, like, physically sighed out loud in the exam room when I brought in my folders and my cross-referenced notes. No matter how many doctors or family members tell me the numbers are fine, they just don't get it. They look at the current digital file on their little tablets and tell me everything is within normal limits and that I need to let it go. But they aren’t looking at the original baseline! They are looking at the altered data. 

I know what I saw. I draw blood for a living, I process these things, I know how to read a comprehensive metabolic panel, and I know for an absolute fact that the chart in the system right now does not match what I saw on the screen the day those labs were originally resulted. I know it doesn't. 

But fighting this... I'll be honest, it is just so incredibly exhausting. It is completely wearing me down. I’m spending every free second I have fighting against this wall of people who refuse to see what is right in front of their faces, and it is draining the life out of me. I'm tired all the time because of it. But I can't just pretend I didn't see what I saw. I am absolutely certain the chart was changed, even if everyone else refuses to admit it and tells me I'm wrong.
Have you ever had thoughts that kept coming back, that you couldn’t control, even when you tried to ignore them or push them away?

Thoughts that I try to push away? No, no, I don't... I don't do that. I mean, why would I try to ignore what's happening? 

My sister—again with my sister, I know, she just has a lot of opinions on how I spend my time—she tells me I'm obsessing and that I need to clear my mind or meditate or whatever. But she doesn't understand the difference between obsessing over nothing and actively investigating a real problem. When I'm thinking about the lab results, it's because I *choose* to think about them. It's not like some random, weird thought just forcing its way into my brain that I can't stop or that I'm trying to get rid of. It's highly focused, deliberate problem-solving. 

Like, for example, the other night I was lying in bed, and I started thinking about the HL7 interface—that's the messaging standard the lab analyzers use to talk to the electronic health record, we use it all the time at the clinic. And I was thinking, okay, if the automated interface was down for maintenance that night, they would have had to enter the metabolic panel results manually. And a manual entry requires a specific user ID and password, it doesn't just cross over automatically from the machine. 

Now, if I had just ignored that thought, or tried to push it away like you're asking, I wouldn't have realized that I need to request the downtime logs from that specific Tuesday. I would have just lost that thread entirely. So I don't push those thoughts away. I got out of bed, I went out to my dining room table, I found my yellow legal pad—the one I use specifically for interface theories, separate from the blue one I use for the timestamps—and I wrote it all down. Every single detail, so I wouldn't forget it by morning. 

So, no, I'm in complete control of my thoughts. I don't have things just popping up that I want to get rid of or that I'm trying to suppress. I actually need every single thought I have right now to figure out how this person covered their tracks in the system. If anything, I wish I had *more* time to think about it, because when I'm at work doing my draws, I have to focus on the patients in my chair, making sure I'm hitting the vein right, labeling the tubes, and I can't give my dad's chart the mental energy it really requires during the day. But yeah, no uncontrollable thoughts here. Just... just very thorough, logical thinking. I don't want to ignore any of it.
Have you ever felt that you had a special ability, mission, or purpose that no one else seemed to understand or recognize?

A special ability? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I don't think I have superpowers or some kind of psychic gift, if that's what you're asking. And I wouldn't call this a "mission," either. That makes it sound like I'm in a spy movie or I think I've been chosen by the universe or something weird like that. I'm really just a normal person. I'm a phlebotomist. 

The only reason I'm the one dealing with all this is simply because I have the background for it. It’s not a special ability, it’s just... it's just basic vocational training. I took classes at the community college, I did my clinical hours, I passed my certification exam. I know the difference between a serum separator tube and an EDTA tube, you know? Like, I know that if you draw a potassium level in a lavender top instead of a gold top, you're going to get a falsely elevated result because of the potassium EDTA in the tube itself. That’s not a special power. That’s just science. That's just my job. 

So when I look at my dad’s chart and I see things that don't add up, it's not because I have some unique, magical insight that no one else possesses. It's just because I actually know how the lab works, from the moment the needle goes into the vein to the moment the centrifuge spins it down and the analyzer spits out the numbers. Anyone with my training would be able to see the exact same things I’m seeing if they just sat down at my dining room table and actually looked at the color-coded highlighters and the timestamps. 

My sister acts like I think I'm on some grand crusade, but I'm really, really not. I don't want a mission. I just want the truth about my dad's lab results. If anything, I wish someone else *would* take over so I wouldn't have to be the one doing all the heavy lifting. If the clinic administrator or the lab director would just sit down and look at the audit trail with me, they’d see it too. So, no, no special purpose or abilities here. Just a daughter who happens to draw blood for a living and knows how to read a metabolic panel. That’s all.
Have you ever had a period of time lasting at least two weeks where you felt persistently down, hopeless, or had very little interest in doing things for most of the day, nearly every day?

Down or hopeless? No. I mean... no, I wouldn't use those words at all. I know I said earlier that I’m exhausted, and I am, I really am completely drained from all the pushback, but being tired isn’t the same thing as being hopeless. Hopeless implies that I’ve given up, right? And I am absolutely not giving up. If I give up, then whoever is messing with my dad’s chart gets away with it, and I just can't let that happen. So there's no hopelessness here, just... just a lot of intense frustration with the people around me. 

And as for losing interest in things? It's honestly the exact opposite. If anything, I have too much going on. I’m still going to work every single day, taking all my regular shifts at the clinic. I still set up my phlebotomy cart every morning with the exact same care I always have—making sure my tourniquets are stocked, checking my alcohol prep pads, organizing the vacutainers by the proper order of draw so I don't cross-contaminate the additives. I'm very meticulous about my job, and I haven't lost a single ounce of interest in doing it right. 

And then when I get home, I don't just lay around in bed staring at the ceiling or crying like someone who's depressed. I get right to work on my dad's case. My sister, she actually tried to pull this exact same line on me the other day. She was like, "You never want to go to Sunday brunch with me anymore, you're isolating yourself, you must be depressed." And I had to explain to her, again, that I'm not depressed, I just don't have three hours to waste eating overpriced waffles and gossiping when I need to be mapping out the network routing from the lab analyzer to the main server. I have a very clear objective right now. I'm highly motivated. 

So no, I haven't had any two weeks where I just didn't care or felt down. I care so much it's basically taking up every waking minute of my day. I don't have time to be hopeless.
Have you ever been absolutely certain of something that turned out to be completely untrue, even after seeing clear proof that it wasn't real?

Untrue? No. No, because what I am certain of is actually the truth, no matter what anyone else tries to tell me. I know exactly what you're getting at with that question, you know. You're talking about the whole reason I'm even here talking to you right now. Because for the past year—an entire year, twelve months of this absolute nightmare—I have been trying to prove that someone inside the clinic system is actively changing, or at the very least holding back, parts of my dad’s lab results. 

And they all think they have "proof" that I'm wrong. No matter how many doctors sit me down in their little consultation rooms with their condescending smiles, or how many family members—like my sister, who I've already told you just refuses to listen—tell me that the numbers are fine, they're completely missing the point. They point to the final electronic health record and say, "Look, the metabolic panel is normal, here's the proof." 

But they aren't looking at the real data. They're looking at the sanitized version. I *know* the chart they are looking at doesn’t match what I originally saw. I saw the initial data pull on the screen before it got scrubbed or altered by whoever has access to the backend. I know what was there. I know what I saw with my own two eyes. 

And honestly, having to fight this battle every single day, having to constantly defend my own memory against people who are just blindly trusting a compromised computer system... it’s wearing me down. It is completely wearing me down to the bone. Because I have to sit there and let them show me this fabricated "proof" that my concerns aren't real, when I know for an absolute fact that they are. I draw blood for a living, I know how these systems work, and I know when a record has been tampered with. So, to answer your question, no. I've never been certain of a lie. I'm just the only one who refuses to accept the lie they're trying to pass off as the truth.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has ever experienced a delusional belief that is not bizarre and is about situations that could occur in real life, such as being followed, poisoned, loved at a distance, or having a disease (non-bizarre delusion), which would support a diagnosis of Delusional Disorder (F22.0).
doctor.question: Have you ever been absolutely certain of something that others say isn’t true, even when there was no clear evidence to support it?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for the past year I’ve been trying to prove that someone in the clinic system is changing or holding back parts of my dad’s lab results, and no matter how many doctors or family members tell me the numbers are fine, I know the chart doesn’t match what I saw and it’s wearing me down.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fixed beliefs that others disagree with and lack clear evidence, which directly corresponds to the definition of delusions.

patient.answer:
Well, see, that’s the thing. You say no clear evidence, but there is evidence, it’s just that no one wants to look at it properly. I mean, this is exactly why I’m even here talking to you in the first place. For the past year—literally an entire twelve months, it started last fall—I have been trying to prove that someone inside the clinic system is either changing or actively holding back parts of my dad’s lab results. 

And everyone, I mean literally everyone, keeps telling me it isn't true. My sister, like I said, she thinks I’m making it all up or seeing things that aren't there. My dad’s primary care doctor actually sighed at me, like, physically sighed out loud in the exam room when I brought in my folders and my cross-referenced notes. No matter how many doctors or family members tell me the numbers are fine, they just don't get it. They look at the current digital file on their little tablets and tell me everything is within normal limits and that I need to let it go. But they aren’t looking at the original baseline! They are looking at the altered data. 

I know what I saw. I draw blood for a living, I process these things, I know how to read a comprehensive metabolic panel, and I know for an absolute fact that the chart in the system right now does not match what I saw on the screen the day those labs were originally resulted. I know it doesn't. 

But fighting this... I'll be honest, it is just so incredibly exhausting. It is completely wearing me down. I’m spending every free second I have fighting against this wall of people who refuse to see what is right in front of their faces, and it is draining the life out of me. I'm tired all the time because of it. But I can't just pretend I didn't see what I saw. I am absolutely certain the chart was changed, even if everyone else refuses to admit it and tells me I'm wrong.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has ever experienced persistent and intrusive thoughts that they cannot control, which may indicate the presence of obsessive-compulsive disorder or other thought disorders.
doctor.question: Have you ever had thoughts that kept coming back, that you couldn’t control, even when you tried to ignore them or push them away?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about intrusive, uncontrollable thoughts (obsessions), which are characteristic of OCD. This is not covered by the patient's symptom profile, which focuses on delusions.

patient.answer:
Thoughts that I try to push away? No, no, I don't... I don't do that. I mean, why would I try to ignore what's happening? 

My sister—again with my sister, I know, she just has a lot of opinions on how I spend my time—she tells me I'm obsessing and that I need to clear my mind or meditate or whatever. But she doesn't understand the difference between obsessing over nothing and actively investigating a real problem. When I'm thinking about the lab results, it's because I *choose* to think about them. It's not like some random, weird thought just forcing its way into my brain that I can't stop or that I'm trying to get rid of. It's highly focused, deliberate problem-solving. 

Like, for example, the other night I was lying in bed, and I started thinking about the HL7 interface—that's the messaging standard the lab analyzers use to talk to the electronic health record, we use it all the time at the clinic. And I was thinking, okay, if the automated interface was down for maintenance that night, they would have had to enter the metabolic panel results manually. And a manual entry requires a specific user ID and password, it doesn't just cross over automatically from the machine. 

Now, if I had just ignored that thought, or tried to push it away like you're asking, I wouldn't have realized that I need to request the downtime logs from that specific Tuesday. I would have just lost that thread entirely. So I don't push those thoughts away. I got out of bed, I went out to my dining room table, I found my yellow legal pad—the one I use specifically for interface theories, separate from the blue one I use for the timestamps—and I wrote it all down. Every single detail, so I wouldn't forget it by morning. 

So, no, I'm in complete control of my thoughts. I don't have things just popping up that I want to get rid of or that I'm trying to suppress. I actually need every single thought I have right now to figure out how this person covered their tracks in the system. If anything, I wish I had *more* time to think about it, because when I'm at work doing my draws, I have to focus on the patients in my chair, making sure I'm hitting the vein right, labeling the tubes, and I can't give my dad's chart the mental energy it really requires during the day. But yeah, no uncontrollable thoughts here. Just... just very thorough, logical thinking. I don't want to ignore any of it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has ever experienced a period of time where they believed they had special powers, abilities, or a unique mission/purpose (to help differentiate schizophrenia spectrum disorders from other conditions like OCD or delusional disorder)
doctor.question: Have you ever felt that you had a special ability, mission, or purpose that no one else seemed to understand or recognize?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about grandiose delusions (special abilities, missions, or purposes), which is not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
A special ability? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I don't think I have superpowers or some kind of psychic gift, if that's what you're asking. And I wouldn't call this a "mission," either. That makes it sound like I'm in a spy movie or I think I've been chosen by the universe or something weird like that. I'm really just a normal person. I'm a phlebotomist. 

The only reason I'm the one dealing with all this is simply because I have the background for it. It’s not a special ability, it’s just... it's just basic vocational training. I took classes at the community college, I did my clinical hours, I passed my certification exam. I know the difference between a serum separator tube and an EDTA tube, you know? Like, I know that if you draw a potassium level in a lavender top instead of a gold top, you're going to get a falsely elevated result because of the potassium EDTA in the tube itself. That’s not a special power. That’s just science. That's just my job. 

So when I look at my dad’s chart and I see things that don't add up, it's not because I have some unique, magical insight that no one else possesses. It's just because I actually know how the lab works, from the moment the needle goes into the vein to the moment the centrifuge spins it down and the analyzer spits out the numbers. Anyone with my training would be able to see the exact same things I’m seeing if they just sat down at my dining room table and actually looked at the color-coded highlighters and the timestamps. 

My sister acts like I think I'm on some grand crusade, but I'm really, really not. I don't want a mission. I just want the truth about my dad's lab results. If anything, I wish someone else *would* take over so I wouldn't have to be the one doing all the heavy lifting. If the clinic administrator or the lab director would just sit down and look at the audit trail with me, they’d see it too. So, no, no special purpose or abilities here. Just a daughter who happens to draw blood for a living and knows how to read a metabolic panel. That’s all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has ever experienced a period of at least two weeks where they felt persistently down, hopeless, or had little interest in doing things for most of the day, nearly every day.
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period of time lasting at least two weeks where you felt persistently down, hopeless, or had very little interest in doing things for most of the day, nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a major depressive episode (persistently down, hopeless, loss of interest), which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Down or hopeless? No. I mean... no, I wouldn't use those words at all. I know I said earlier that I’m exhausted, and I am, I really am completely drained from all the pushback, but being tired isn’t the same thing as being hopeless. Hopeless implies that I’ve given up, right? And I am absolutely not giving up. If I give up, then whoever is messing with my dad’s chart gets away with it, and I just can't let that happen. So there's no hopelessness here, just... just a lot of intense frustration with the people around me. 

And as for losing interest in things? It's honestly the exact opposite. If anything, I have too much going on. I’m still going to work every single day, taking all my regular shifts at the clinic. I still set up my phlebotomy cart every morning with the exact same care I always have—making sure my tourniquets are stocked, checking my alcohol prep pads, organizing the vacutainers by the proper order of draw so I don't cross-contaminate the additives. I'm very meticulous about my job, and I haven't lost a single ounce of interest in doing it right. 

And then when I get home, I don't just lay around in bed staring at the ceiling or crying like someone who's depressed. I get right to work on my dad's case. My sister, she actually tried to pull this exact same line on me the other day. She was like, "You never want to go to Sunday brunch with me anymore, you're isolating yourself, you must be depressed." And I had to explain to her, again, that I'm not depressed, I just don't have three hours to waste eating overpriced waffles and gossiping when I need to be mapping out the network routing from the lab analyzer to the main server. I have a very clear objective right now. I'm highly motivated. 

So no, I haven't had any two weeks where I just didn't care or felt down. I care so much it's basically taking up every waking minute of my day. I don't have time to be hopeless.

patient.answer:
Untrue? No. No, because what I am certain of is actually the truth, no matter what anyone else tries to tell me. I know exactly what you're getting at with that question, you know. You're talking about the whole reason I'm even here talking to you right now. Because for the past year—an entire year, twelve months of this absolute nightmare—I have been trying to prove that someone inside the clinic system is actively changing, or at the very least holding back, parts of my dad’s lab results. 

And they all think they have "proof" that I'm wrong. No matter how many doctors sit me down in their little consultation rooms with their condescending smiles, or how many family members—like my sister, who I've already told you just refuses to listen—tell me that the numbers are fine, they're completely missing the point. They point to the final electronic health record and say, "Look, the metabolic panel is normal, here's the proof." 

But they aren't looking at the real data. They're looking at the sanitized version. I *know* the chart they are looking at doesn’t match what I originally saw. I saw the initial data pull on the screen before it got scrubbed or altered by whoever has access to the backend. I know what was there. I know what I saw with my own two eyes. 

And honestly, having to fight this battle every single day, having to constantly defend my own memory against people who are just blindly trusting a compromised computer system... it’s wearing me down. It is completely wearing me down to the bone. Because I have to sit there and let them show me this fabricated "proof" that my concerns aren't real, when I know for an absolute fact that they are. I draw blood for a living, I know how these systems work, and I know when a record has been tampered with. So, to answer your question, no. I've never been certain of a lie. I'm just the only one who refuses to accept the lie they're trying to pass off as the truth.
